title: Burst queue behavior and reserved GPU capacity deep dive
summary: SE-led technical deep dive focused on burst policies, queueing models, and reserved GPU sizing for Cloudline Health's mixed workload (interactive chat + nightly embeddings). Discussed KV cache behavior, batching tradeoffs, quantization options for cost/latency, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed next steps: Redwood to run a capacity calc, share benchmark spreadsheet, and schedule a pilot with reserved pool + burst window.
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jamie from Redwood, and with me is Sofia and Liam. We're planning to nerd out on burst behaviour and reserved capacity sizing. We have about an hour, is that still good for everyone?
[00:10] Rajesh Patel: Yep that works. We want to understand how to keep the chat latency under 200ms p90 while also supporting nightly embedding jobs that spike.
[00:20] Sofia Martinez: Great. Quick orientation — Cloudline gave us their rough RPS profile, right? Maya, you sent the per-route percentiles?
[00:26] Maya Lin: Yeah uploaded it to the shared drive, link in the invite. There are two big patterns: interactive chat during business hours — short sequences, high QPS bursts — and batch embedding runs overnight that push a lot of tokens for long-context models.
[00:39] Tim O'Neill: And we have a VPC-only requirement for PHI, so the private deployment path is mandatory for the initial pilot.
[00:45] Sofia Martinez: OK noted. So on Redwood's side when we talk about burst policies we mean two things: 1) short-term overprovisioning that lets you exceed the reserved throughput for a window and 2) an enqueue/backpressure model when sustained load exceeds capacity. We'll draw both.
[01:02] Liam O'Connor: I'll share my screen — here's a simplified queue model: requests arrive, per-route token buckets track allocation, if reserved pool has headroom they go directly to model shards; if not, they either enter a short queue (soft queue with TTL) or trigger burst instances if burst budget available.
[01:18] [screen noise]
[01:22] Rajesh Patel: Can you explain burst budget — is it per-customer or per-pool?
[01:26] Sofia Martinez: Per-customer and per-pool. You configure a reserve (committed GPU units) and then a burst allowance measured in GPU-seconds or GPU-minutes per billing period. So you can tolerate a 3x surge for N minutes before we start shedding.
[01:40] Sara Gomez: How do you guarantee isolation? If my neighbor on the same physical host spikes, could that affect our latency?
[01:46] Priya Desai: For Dedicated / Private we give you an isolated pool of GPUs. If you're on host-shared infra (hosted tier) there is soft isolation via cgroups and NVML enforcement; but for VPC/private we recommend reserved pools to avoid noisy neighbor concerns.
[02:00] Victor Huang: One risk: when a spike causes the KV cache to get evicted frequently, we saw latency tail-chop — cold KV misses add like 20-40ms per token in our tests. How does Redwood handle prefix/KV cache eviction gracefully?
[02:14] Sofia Martinez: Good observation. We maintain LRU-per-shard for KV items and have a dynamic hotlist that pins top prefixes based on recency and cost-benefit heuristics. If eviction happens during a spike we can route requests to a warmed standby replica that keeps a fuller KV set, but that costs burst memory.
[02:33] Rajesh Patel: So pinned prefixes — is that configurable? Could we pin diagnostically-sensitive prefixes in case of privacy regs?
[02:40] Sara Gomez: Yeah, like session tokens? We need to ensure eviction doesn't leak tokens.
[02:44] Sofia Martinez: You can pin at the tenant level, and we expose flags in the private agent to prevent persistence to disk; KV entries are in-memory and encrypted with your KMS keys.
[02:55] Maya Lin: Quick question on batching: our embedding jobs prefer larger batch sizes for throughput, but chat wants small batches for low latency. How do you reconcile both on a shared pool?
[03:05] Liam O'Connor: We do adaptive batching: the router groups compatible requests within a latency budget. For chat routes we set per-request latency SLOs and max batch windows of ~10-20ms, while batch embedding routes can tolerate 500-2000ms windows and much larger batch sizes. The runtime schedules batches onto GPU microbatches to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[03:25] Tim O'Neill: But that still means embeddings could starve chat if the scheduler is naive.
[03:29] Sofia Martinez: Exactly. Solution: priority lanes — chat gets higher priority and guaranteed fraction of GPU cores and token throughput. Also preemptible embedding workers that yield on priority traffic. We also use token-level rate shaping so embeddings only use leftover capacity.
[03:45] Rajesh Patel: Can you share numbers? If we reserve 4 A100s, what's the expected p50/p95/p99 for a 7B model with int8 quantization versus fp16?
[03:56] Priya Desai: Rough ballpark — for a 7B LLM on A100 w/ fp16 we see ~6-9ms per token p50 depending on sequence length, p95 around 25-40ms, p99 around 80-120ms. With int8 quant or int4 quant we can reduce p95 by ~20-35% but there's model-specific accuracy tradeoffs. For chat with short sequences (<=64 tokens) on a 4-GPU reserved pool, you can hit 150-200ms p95 across many concurrent sessions if batching windows are tuned.
[04:26] Maya Lin: What about KV cache size when quantized? Does INT8 affect KV memory layout?
[04:31] Sofia Martinez: Quantized KV storage is smaller but access patterns are the same; however certain quantization schemes require dequantization during attention which adds CPU/memory overhead. For very high QPS interactive workloads we often keep KV in FP16 for latency-sensitive hot sessions and quantize longer-tail states.
[04:48] Victor Huang: Is there any automatic recommendation tool? Our infra team hates manually tuning windows.
[04:53] Priya Desai: Redwood Optimize gives suggestions — it analyzes your traffic traces and proposes batch windows, reserved pool sizes, and quant profiles with estimated cost/latency impact. We'll run a quick capacity calc for you as a starting point.
[05:05] [pause]
[05:07] Rajesh Patel: Concerning the enqueue model — what happens if the soft queue fills up? Do you shed, backpressure the client, or spin up more burst instances?
[05:16] Liam O'Connor: There's a prioritized lifecycle: 1) try to allocate from reserve 2) use burst budget 3) enqueue up to soft-queue TTL (default 5s) 4) if still over threshold, we return a 429 with backoff hints. In Private we can automate extra capacity spin-up but it depends on your cloud infra — we can trigger your autoscaler with a webhook.
[05:33] Tim O'Neill: Our cloud account uses a constrained GPU quota. Can Redwood spin GPUs in a different region as a fallback? We're region-locked for compliance.
[05:41] Sofia Martinez: Fallback across regions violates your data residency/VPC constraints. For Private you can configure a cold standby in an approved region, but data residency controls must be explicit. For strictly on-prem or VPC-in-restricted regions you should size reserved plus small burst budget.
[06:00] Sara Gomez: Security question — does the burst mechanism cause any logs or KV snapshots to be sent to shared telemetry? We're under HIPAA audits.
[06:08] Priya Desai: No telemetry payloads include only anonymized metrics for platform health unless you opt-in. KV and model state never leave your private deployment; logs are delivered to your logging endpoint and can be disabled. We'll include SOC2/ISO docs.
[06:19] Maya Lin: Let's talk numbers again — give us a worked example. We have a peak interactive burst of 600 concurrent sessions each sending 1 req every 8s on average. Nightly embedding run is 200 concurrent users for 2 hours processing ~5M tokens per hour.
[06:34] Liam O'Connor: OK quick calc roughs: interactive steady-state rps = 600/8 = 75 RPS. If each request generates ~60 tokens, that's 4.5k tokens/s. With a 7B fp16 model on one A100 you might do ~6k tokens/s (very roughly), but that's peak throughput when saturated and without other work. We recommend reserving 2 GPUs to hit headroom at p95. For the nightly embedding 5M tokens/hr is ~1.4k tokens/s sustained; that could be handled by the same pool but you'd want burst isolation because embeddings will consume batch windows and might increase cold-KV misses.
[07:10] Rajesh Patel: So recommended: reserve 4 GPUs with a 30-minute burst budget and priority lane favoring chat?
[07:16] Sofia Martinez: That sounds reasonable as a conservative starting point. We'll validate with an experiment: a 2-4-peak test where we simulate chat bursts and run embedding workers to see interference.
[07:25] Victor Huang: On the pilot, can we start with a small reserved pool on-prem and then scale to dedicated in-cloud later?
[07:31] Priya Desai: Yes — Redwood Private supports hybrid: we ship a control plane in your VPC and can point to on-prem inference nodes plus cloud GPUs. You can reassign capacity as you transition.
[07:40] Maya Lin: One more on quantization: our model owner is concerned about logits drift. Have you seen production regressions with int4 for instruction-following models?
[07:48] Sofia Martinez: Sometimes. Int8 is pretty safe for many 7B/13B families; int4 can introduce small fidelity regressions, especially on token-limited prompts. We recommend running your eval harnesses — Redwood Optimize can run those on candidate quantized variants and surface changes in logprobs or eval metrics.
[08:05] Rajesh Patel: Cool. Let's talk SLA: if we reserve 4 GPUs and we get a 99.9% uptime guarantee, what about latency SLOs?
[08:13] Jamie Park: SLA covers availability of the pool; latency SLOs are best-effort but we provide historical p95/p99 dashboards per route and will add a performance SLA into the enterprise contract if needed.
[08:24] Tim O'Neill: Any gotchas with the private agent and our KMS? We use Azure Key Vault with customer-managed keys.
[08:31] Priya Desai: Works fine; the private agent integrates with your KMS via standard interfaces. We'll need a short network diagram and some firewall rules for the control-plane connectivity.
[08:40] [chatter about scheduling a pilot — jamie types in chat link]
[08:45] Jamie Park: I'll drop the benchmark spreadsheet and the capacity calc, plus a notional pilot runbook into the shared drive.
[08:52] Maya Lin: For pilot success criteria: keep chat p95 under 200ms during a 1-hour 3x burst, and embeddings complete within target throughput with no more than 5% increase in chat tail latency.
[09:03] Sofia Martinez: Got it — we'll build test harness.
[09:05] Rajesh Patel: Anything else — procurement or compliance?
[09:08] Sara Gomez: Send SOC2/ISO and a sketch of the dataflow for PHI.
[09:12] Jamie Park: We'll include those docs and the action items. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up.
[09:17] [END]
